traditions.name: Dravidian village and guardian-deity worship
traditions.earliest_attestation: Sangam literature (c. 1st–3rd c. CE) for Murugan/Korravai; village cults attested in medieval inscriptions
traditions.geographic_origin: Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra (South India)
traditions.scholarly_note: Grama-devata and kaval-deivam (guardian) worship, often with non-Brahmin priests and blood offering; continuously interwoven with Sanskritic Hinduism.

traditions.name: Ayyavazhi
traditions.scholarly_note: Treated by adherents as a distinct dharma; Indian census classes it under Hinduism. Scriptures: Akilathirattu Ammanai and Arul Nool.

traditions.name: Lingayat / Virashaiva
traditions.earliest_attestation: 12th c. CE (Basava and the Vachana poets)
traditions.scholarly_note: Devotion to Shiva as the personal linga worn on the body (ishtalinga); rejects caste and temple ritual in its founding vachanas.

traditions.name: Ahom (Tai-Ahom traditional religion)
traditions.earliest_attestation: 13th c. CE (Ahom kingdom founded 1228); Ahom Buranjis
traditions.geographic_origin: Assam (Brahmaputra valley), from Tai migrants out of Mong Mao
traditions.scholarly_note: Tai religion of the Ahom dynasty, with Phura and the heavenly Lengdon; later blended with Assamese Hinduism; revived ritual (Me-Dam-Me-Phi) today.

traditions.name: Kalasha traditional religion
traditions.earliest_attestation: Oral tradition; first ethnographic records 19th–20th c. CE; roots in archaic Indo-Iranian / Nuristani religion
traditions.scholarly_note: The last living continuation of pre-Islamic Hindu Kush polytheism; closely related to the Nuristani ('Kafir') pantheon headed by Imra.

traditions.name: Newar religion (Kathmandu Valley)
traditions.earliest_attestation: Licchavi inscriptions (5th–9th c. CE); Malla period cults (12th–18th c. CE)
traditions.scholarly_note: Newar Buddhism (Vajrayana with Sanskrit liturgy) and Newar Hinduism share deities, festivals and priests.

traditions.name: Kazakh and Kyrgyz folk religion
traditions.earliest_attestation: Orkhon-era Turkic substrate (8th c. CE); epic and folk records 19th c. CE
traditions.scholarly_note: Tengrist and shamanic substrate blended with folk Islam: patron-spirits of herds, ancestor veneration (aruak), and demonic beings.

traditions.name: Bactrian / Kushan pantheon
traditions.earliest_attestation: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka (c. 127–190 CE); Rabatak inscription
traditions.geographic_origin: Bactria and Gandhara (Afghanistan, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan)
traditions.scholarly_note: An Iranian pantheon written in Bactrian on Kushan coins, alongside Greek, Indian and Buddhist deities; the most explicit ancient record of East Iranian gods.

traditions.name: Sakha (Yakut) Aiyy faith
traditions.scholarly_note: Three-world cosmology: Aiyy deities of the Upper World, abaasy of the upper and lower worlds; revived today as Aiyy Yeürekhe (Tengrism of the Sakha).

traditions.name: Evenki shamanic religion
traditions.geographic_origin: Central and eastern Siberia, Amur region
traditions.scholarly_note: Origin home of the word 'shaman' (Evenki saman); three-world cosmology joined by a clan river.

traditions.name: Khanty and Mansi (Ob-Ugrian) religion
traditions.earliest_attestation: Ethnographic records 18th–20th c. CE; bear-festival songs
traditions.geographic_origin: Ob and Irtysh basins, Western Siberia
traditions.scholarly_note: Phratry system (Por and Mos), sky father Num-Torum, the bear festival and sacred-place spirits.

traditions.name: Nenets religion
traditions.geographic_origin: Yamal and the tundra of northwestern Siberia
traditions.scholarly_note: Samoyedic sky-god Num and underworld Nga; sacred sites (khekhe) and reindeer sacrifice.

traditions.name: Chukchi, Koryak and Itelmen religion
traditions.earliest_attestation: Ethnographic records 18th–20th c. CE (Steller, Krasheninnikov; Jesup North Pacific Expedition)
traditions.geographic_origin: Chukotka and Kamchatka, far northeastern Siberia
traditions.scholarly_note: Raven creator-trickster cycles shared across the Bering Strait with Northwest Coast and Inuit peoples; domestic shamanism and kelet spirits.

deities.summary: Father Sky, the shining heaven. With Mother Earth (Pṛthivī) he is the primeval parent-pair of gods and men, invoked together as Dyāvāpṛthivī. Father of Uṣas, Agni, Indra and the Aśvins, he is a remote presence whose place in worship has passed to his sons.
deities.etymology: Sanskrit dyaús 'sky, day' + pitṛ 'father', from PIE *dyēus ph2tēr 'sky-father'

deities.summary: The broad Earth, mother of all beings. With Dyaus she forms the cosmic parents; the Atharvaveda's great Earth Hymn praises her as the bearer of mountains, plants, waters and every people, who is asked to forgive the wounds of the plough.
deities.etymology: Sanskrit pṛthivī 'the broad one', from PIE *pleth2-wih2 'broad (earth)'

deities.summary: The golden Impeller who rouses all beings to motion at dawn and lays them to rest at dusk. The Gāyatrī mantra, the most recited verse of the Veda, is addressed to him: 'May we meditate on the excellent radiance of the god Savitṛ; may he stimulate our thoughts.'

Guardian of roads, herds and journeys; finder of lost cattle and lost things. Drawn by goats and eating gruel because he is toothless, he guides the traveller on earth and the dead on the path to the fathers.
An Āditya, companion of Mitra and Varuṇa, guardian of hospitality, the bonds of the Ārya community, marriage and the road. In later tradition he is chief of the Pitṛs (ancestors).
The Āditya who apportions each person's share of wealth and fortune, invoked at dawn for prosperity and marital happiness.
The thundering rain-cloud, a bull who impregnates the earth with rain; at his coming the winds blow, lightning flies and plants spring up.

Lord of creatures, the creator who in the beginning was alone, desired to be many, heated himself in tapas and emitted the worlds, gods and beings. Exhausted and fallen apart after creation, he is reassembled in the Vedic fire-altar — every sacrifice restores the creator.

The Golden Embryo arising in the beginning on the cosmic waters, sole lord of all that is born, who holds earth and sky. In the Purāṇas the world-egg floats on the waters and Brahmā is born within it.
iconography: golden egg on the cosmic waters

deities.summary: Trita the Third, son of the waters, who with Indra's aid slays the three-headed, six-eyed Viśvarūpa son of Tvaṣṭṛ and frees the cattle; a hero cast into a well who calls on the gods from its depths.
The Child of the Waters: fire that shines within the waters without fuel, golden, surrounded by the maternal waters who nourish him. He is the hidden fire of lightning and of the depths.
The rock-cave enclosure in which the Paṇis hid the stolen cows of dawn. Indra and Bṛhaspati with the Aṅgiras singers split Vala by the power of the chant and released the cattle and the light.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th–6th c. CE (Devī Māhātmya); earlier Mahiṣa in epic
deities.summary: The buffalo-asura who, by a boon that no man or god could kill him, conquered heaven and drove out the devas. From the gods' combined fury the Goddess arose, and on the tenth day she cut off his head as he emerged from the buffalo's body. Navarātri and Durgā Pūjā celebrate his defeat.

Daitya king, son of Kaśyapa and Diti, who won a boon that he could be killed neither by man nor beast, by day nor night, indoors nor out, on earth nor in the sky, by no weapon. He tormented his son Prahlāda for worshipping Viṣṇu, until Narasiṃha burst from a pillar at dusk and slew him on his lap at the threshold.
Brother of Hiraṇyakaśipu who dragged the Earth down into the cosmic ocean; Viṣṇu as the boar Varāha dived, slew him and lifted the Earth on his tusks.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1st millennium BCE (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.2.5 three-steps motif); epic and Purāṇas
deities.summary: The generous asura king, grandson of Prahlāda, under whom all lived in equality and plenty. When the dwarf Vāmana begged three paces of land, Bali kept his word, and Viṣṇu in cosmic form covered earth and sky and placed the third step on Bali's head, sending him to rule Sutala. Each year at Onam he returns to visit his people.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 4th–2nd c. BCE (Saṅkarṣaṇa-Vāsudeva coins of Agathocles, c. 180 BCE)
deities.summary: Elder brother of Kṛṣṇa, the plough-bearing strongman, avatāra of the serpent Śeṣa (and in some lists the eighth avatar of Viṣṇu). He diverted the Yamunā with his plough and taught both Bhīma and Duryodhana the mace.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 12th c. CE (Puri temple by Anantavarman Chodaganga); earlier local cult
deities.summary: The Lord of the Universe at Puri, worshipped with his brother Balabhadra and sister Subhadrā in wooden forms with great round eyes. Every year the three ride in towering chariots in the Ratha Yātrā; every 12–19 years the images are renewed (Nabakalebara) as the divine essence passes into new wood.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 13th c. CE (Pandharpur inscriptions; Jñāneśvar, Nāmdev)
deities.summary: Viṭhoba of Pandharpur, a form of Kṛṣṇa who stands on a brick with hands on his hips, waiting for his devotees. He came to see the devotee Puṇḍalīka, who, busy serving his parents, tossed him a brick to stand on; he has stood there ever since. The Vārkarī pilgrims walk to him every Āṣāḍhī Ekādaśī.

deities.earliest_attestation: Inscriptions at Tirumala from c. 9th c. CE; Āḻvār hymns (6th–9th c. CE)
deities.summary: Viṣṇu as Lord of the Venkaṭa hill at Tirumala, who came to earth in the Kali age and borrowed from Kubera to fund his wedding to Padmāvatī; devotees offer their hair and wealth to help repay the debt. His temple is among the most visited shrines on earth.

deities.earliest_attestation: Sabarimala tradition; Sastha worship attested in Kerala inscriptions from c. 9th–10th c. CE
deities.summary: Ayyappan, son of Śiva and Viṣṇu in the form of Mohinī, born to destroy the buffalo-demoness Mahiṣī. Raised as prince Maṇikaṇṭhan of Pandalam, he took his seat as a celibate yogi on the Sabarimala hill, where pilgrims who keep a 41-day vow climb the eighteen holy steps.

Khaṇḍobā of Jejuri, a warrior form of Śiva (Mārtaṇḍa Bhairava) who rides a horse with his wife Mhāḷsā, slaying the demons Maṇi and Malla. His devotees shower turmeric (bhandara) until the hill turns gold; dogs are his companions.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1500 BCE (Rigveda); temples c. 5th–13th c. CE (Konark, Modhera)
deities.summary: The Sun, eye of Mitra and Varuṇa, driving his chariot of seven horses with Aruṇa as charioteer; first of the Navagrahas. Saura devotees worshipped him as the supreme god; Chhath and Makara Saṅkrānti still honour him.

The Moon, identified with Soma, married to the twenty-seven Nakṣatras, daughters of Dakṣa. Cursed by Dakṣa to waste away for favouring Rohiṇī, he wanes and is restored by Śiva, who wears him as a crescent.
Mars among the Navagrahas, red son of the Earth (Bhūmi), warrior and commander of the planetary army.
Lord of the sacred word and preceptor (guru) of the gods; with the chant he split the Vala cave. As the planet Jupiter he is the great benefic of the Navagrahas.

deities.earliest_attestation: Vedic (Uśanā Kāvya, RV); epic and Purāṇas
deities.summary: Preceptor of the asuras, master of the Mṛtasañjīvanī art that revives the dead; as the planet Venus he grants beauty, wealth and pleasure.

Saturn, son of Sūrya and Chāyā, dark and slow-moving, whose gaze brings hardship as the reward of karma. His seven-and-a-half-year transit (sāḍe sātī) is feared; he is propitiated on Saturdays with oil and black sesame, and devotees of Hanumān are spared his torment.

deities.earliest_attestation: Svarbhānu in Rigveda 5.40; Rāhu in epic and Purāṇas
deities.summary: The severed head of the asura Svarbhānu who stole a sip of amṛta at the churning of the ocean. Sūrya and Candra exposed him; Viṣṇu's discus cut off his head, but the nectar had made it immortal. In revenge Rāhu swallows the sun and moon at eclipse.
The headless body of Svarbhānu, the descending lunar node; a shadow planet of detachment, comets and liberation.
The nine 'seizers' that govern human fate: Sūrya, Candra, Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śani, Rāhu and Ketu. They are installed in shrines in a 3×3 grid and propitiated in graha-śānti rites.

The heavenly river who descended to earth at the prayer of King Bhagīratha to purify the ashes of his ancestors; Śiva caught her in his hair to break her fall. To bathe in her erases sin, and ashes cast in her waters reach heaven.

The thousand-headed serpent king, 'the Remainder' who survives the dissolution of the worlds. He bears the earth on his hoods and is the couch on which Viṣṇu sleeps on the cosmic ocean; he incarnates as Lakṣmaṇa and Balarāma.
Nāga king who served as the churning rope wound around Mount Mandara when gods and asuras churned the ocean for amṛta; the poison he spewed was swallowed by Śiva. He coils around Śiva's neck.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1st millennium BCE (Vedic sarpa; Buddhist and Jain texts); Bharhut reliefs (2nd c. BCE)
deities.summary: Semi-divine serpent beings dwelling in Pātāla, lakes and springs, guardians of waters, rain and treasure. Children of Kaśyapa and Kadrū, enemies of Garuḍa; honoured at Nāga Pañcamī and in serpent groves (sarpa kāvu).

King of birds, son of Kaśyapa and Vinatā, who stole the amṛta from the gods to free his mother from slavery to the serpents, and became Viṣṇu's mount. Enemy of the nāgas, invoked against snake poison.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th c. BCE–4th c. CE (Rāmāyaṇa); Vedic Sītā (furrow goddess)
deities.summary: Born from a furrow ploughed by King Janaka, wife of Rāma and incarnation of Lakṣmī. Abducted by Rāvaṇa, faithful through captivity and trial by fire, she finally returned into the Earth her mother.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 12th c. CE (Gīta Govinda); earlier Prakrit verse (Gāthā Saptaśatī)
primary_sources: Writings of the Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana
deities.summary: The cowherd beloved of Kṛṣṇa in Vṛndāvana, supreme among the gopīs. For the Gauḍīya and Nimbārka schools she is Kṛṣṇa's own bliss-energy (hlādinī śakti), the goddess of devotion whose love surpasses all.
The divine sage who wanders the three worlds with his vīṇā singing 'Nārāyaṇa'; messenger of the gods, teacher of bhakti, and a mischief-maker whose quarrels always serve a divine purpose.
Son of the sage Atri and Anasūyā, in whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva became one; the wandering avadhūta guru who learned from twenty-four teachers in nature, followed by four dogs and a cow.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 13th c. CE (Bengali Maṅgal-kāvya); earlier serpent cults
deities.summary: Goddess of snakes in Bengal and the east, who protects from snakebite and grants fertility. The merchant Chand Sadagar refused her worship until she killed his sons; his daughter-in-law Behulā floated her husband's corpse downriver to win him back, and Chand at last offered her a flower with his left hand.

deities.earliest_attestation: Medieval (Skanda Purāṇa); folk cult widespread in North India
deities.summary: The 'Cool One', goddess of smallpox and pustular disease, riding a donkey with broom, winnowing fan and pot of cool water. She both visits the disease and cools it away; she is worshipped with cold food on Śītalā Aṣṭamī.
The physician of the gods who rose from the churning of the ocean bearing the pot of amṛta; an avatāra of Viṣṇu and the founder of Āyurveda, worshipped on Dhanteras.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 6th–8th c. CE (Kāpālika and Purāṇic sources)
deities.summary: The terrifying form of Śiva who sprang from his wrath and cut off Brahmā's fifth head for its arrogance. Bearing the skull stuck to his hand, he wandered as a beggar until it fell at Kāśī, where he is now kotwal, the city's guardian. His mount is a black dog.
The fierce warrior born from a lock of Śiva's hair when Satī immolated herself at Dakṣa's sacrifice; he destroyed the sacrifice and beheaded Dakṣa.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1st millennium CE (bull emblem of Śiva earlier, Kushan coins)
deities.summary: The bull who is Śiva's mount, gatekeeper of Kailāsa and chief of the gaṇas; he sits facing the sanctum of every Śiva temple, and devotees whisper their wishes in his ear.

deities.earliest_attestation: Kushan period images (1st–3rd c. CE); Devī Māhātmya (5th–6th c. CE)
deities.summary: The seven Mothers — Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī and Cāmuṇḍā — the śaktis who emerged from the gods to fight the demon Raktabīja, drinking his blood before each drop could spawn new demons.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 10th–15th c. CE (Śākta Purāṇas and Tantras)
deities.summary: Ten forms of the Great Goddess — Kālī, Tārā, Tripurasundarī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalāmukhī, Mātaṅgī and Kamalā — which Satī displayed to Śiva, surrounding him on all ten directions, when he forbade her to attend Dakṣa's sacrifice.

Daughter of Dakṣa and first wife of Śiva, who gave up her body in the fire of her father's sacrifice when Śiva was insulted. Śiva wandered with her corpse until Viṣṇu's discus cut it apart; the places where her body fell became the Śakti Pīṭhas. She was reborn as Pārvatī.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 7th–8th c. CE (Kāmarūpa inscriptions); Kālikā Purāṇa (c. 10th c. CE)
deities.summary: The Goddess of desire on Nīlācala hill in Assam, worshipped as a yoni-shaped stone where Satī's womb fell. Each year during Ambubācī the goddess menstruates and the temple closes for three days.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 7th–9th c. CE (Tamil inscriptions of Sāttan/Sāstā)
deities.summary: Guardian god of the Tamil village boundary, riding out each night on a horse or elephant to protect the fields, with his consorts Pūraṇā and Puṣkalā. Villagers dedicate terracotta horses to him, often of enormous size.
iconography: seated with one leg raised by a strap (yogapaṭṭa)

deities.summary: The great mother goddess of Tamil villages, bringer of rain and of pox. The 'pearls' of smallpox are her grace and her anger; at her festivals devotees walk on fire, carry fire-pots and pierce themselves in vow.

deities.earliest_attestation: Medieval (Saundatti temple, c. 12th–13th c. CE); Renukā in epic
deities.summary: Mother of Paraśurāma, beheaded at her husband Jamadagni's order and restored to life. Worshipped at Saundatti in Karnataka and across the Deccan as Yellammā, 'mother of all', with her headless and head-only forms; her devotees include the jogappa and jogati.
A fierce Tamil guardian deity, regarded as a form of Śiva, who protects villages, roads and homes against evil spirits and thieves; he receives offerings of meat, toddy and cigars.
The black guardian god, chief of the kaval deivam, armed with a sickle (aruval), riding a horse; he upholds justice, punishes oath-breakers and protects the villages of southern Tamil Nadu.

Vaikuṇḍar, the incarnation of Nārāyaṇa born of the sea at Tiruchendur in 1833, the final avatāra who destroys Kali (the evil of the age). He gathered the oppressed of Travancore, abolished caste distinctions at the well and the temple, and established the Dharma Yukam.

The primordial evil born at the beginning of creation, a monstrous being of mountainous size. Cut into fragments by Nārāyaṇa, each fragment was reborn as an enemy of righteousness in each age — Ravana, Duryodhana — and last as Kaliyan, the spirit of the Kali Yuga.

primary_sources: Vachanas of Basava, Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahadevi
deities.summary: Śiva the formless Lord worn by each devotee on the body as the personal liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga). The Lingayat needs no temple or priest: 'the body is the temple'. The vachana poets call him by personal names — Kūḍalasaṅgama, Cennamallikārjuna, Guhēśvara.

Statesman-saint of Kalyāṇa who founded the Anubhava Maṇṭapa, a hall of spiritual dialogue open to all castes and to women. Lingayats revere him as the founder of their faith, regarded by many as an incarnation of Nandī.
The formless supreme creator of the Tai-Ahom, who existed alone in the void and created the world, the gods and humankind.

King of heaven in Ahom religion, god of thunder and rain, who sent his grandsons Khunlung and Khunlai down to earth by a golden ladder to rule; from them descend the Ahom kings (Swargadeos, 'lords of heaven').

The two divine brothers sent down from heaven by Lengdon, who descended at Mong-Ri-Mong-Ram and founded the Tai kingdoms; ancestors of the Ahom royal line and founders of the Me-Dam-Me-Phi ancestor rites.

deities.earliest_attestation: Gandharan reliefs (1st–3rd c. CE); Pāli Ambaṭṭha Sutta (as Vajirapāṇi yakkha)
deities.summary: The thunderbolt-bearing bodhisattva, protector and constant companion of the Buddha, who embodies the power of all Buddhas. In the Pāli canon a yakkha with a blazing vajra stands over those who would refuse the Buddha's question; in Vajrayāna he is the wrathful lord of secrets who subdues the obstacle-makers.

Guardian kings of the four quarters dwelling on the slopes of Mount Meru: Dhṛtarāṣṭra (east, gandharvas), Virūḍhaka (south, kumbhāṇḍas), Virūpākṣa (west, nāgas) and Vaiśravaṇa (north, yakṣas). They protect the Dharma and the world, and stand at the gates of temples across Asia.

deities.earliest_attestation: Pāli canon; Gandharan and Central Asian images
deities.summary: Guardian King of the North and lord of the yakṣas, giver of wealth and protector of the Dharma; carrying a banner or stūpa and a mongoose spitting jewels. In Khotan he was royal ancestor; in Japan Bishamonten is a god of war and fortune.

Sakka, lord of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three on the summit of Meru, a devout follower of the Buddha who questions him on the Dharma, protects the virtuous and attained stream-entry. He received the Buddha's hair at the renunciation and attended the descent from Tāvatiṃsa.

The great Brahmā who, when the newly awakened Buddha hesitated to teach, descended and begged him to open the doors of the Deathless for beings with little dust in their eyes. In the Brahmajāla Sutta another Mahābrahmā wrongly believes himself the creator.

deities.earliest_attestation: Gandharan sculpture (2nd–3rd c. CE); Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya
deities.summary: A yakṣiṇī mother of five hundred children who stole and devoured the children of Rājagṛha. The Buddha hid her youngest son Priyaṅkara under his alms-bowl; feeling a mother's grief she converted and became protector of children and childbirth, fed daily from the monks' alms.

deities.earliest_attestation: 8th c. CE (Samye); biographies from 12th c. CE
primary_sources: Zangling-ma (terma biography revealed by Nyangral Nyima Özer)
deities.summary: The Lotus-Born master from Oḍḍiyāna, invited to Tibet by King Trisong Detsen, who bound the hostile spirits of Tibet under oath to protect the Dharma, founded Samye monastery and hid treasure-teachings (terma) for future ages. The Nyingma revere him as the Second Buddha.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 8th c. CE (Samye tradition); later Nechung oracle
deities.summary: A powerful worldly spirit-king bound by Padmasambhava to guard the treasury of Samye, later seated at Nechung, where he speaks through the State Oracle of Tibet.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 12th–15th c. CE (epic in oral performance)
primary_sources: Epic of King Gesar (Tibetan oral epic)
deities.summary: The divine warrior-king sent down from heaven to Ling to subdue the demon kings of the four directions, defend the weak and establish the Dharma. Bards (drungpa) receive the epic in visions; he is invoked as a war god and as a coming saviour.

deities.earliest_attestation: Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra (Gilgit manuscripts, c. 6th–7th c. CE; Chinese 4th–7th c. CE)
deities.summary: The Medicine Buddha of lapis-lazuli light, lord of the eastern Pure Land Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa, who vowed twelve great vows to heal the sick in body and mind and to cure the poison of ignorance.

deities.earliest_attestation: Aṣṭasāhasrikā (c. 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE); goddess images c. 9th–12th c. CE (Pala)
deities.summary: The Perfection of Wisdom personified as a serene goddess holding a book and a lotus; she is the insight into emptiness from which every Buddha is born.

The five Buddha-families of the vajra maṇḍala — Vairocana (centre), Akṣobhya (east), Ratnasambhava (south), Amitābha (west) and Amoghasiddhi (north) — who embody the five wisdoms that transform the five poisons and the five aggregates.

The nāga king who, during a seven-day storm in the weeks after the Awakening, coiled seven times around the meditating Buddha and spread his hood over his head, then took the form of a young man and bowed.
iconography: seven-headed cobra hood over the seated Buddha

deities.earliest_attestation: Kalpa Sūtra (c. 4th–5th c. CE redaction); Mathura images (Kushan period)
deities.summary: The first Tīrthaṅkara of our cycle, who taught humanity agriculture, writing, crafts and the social order when the wish-fulfilling trees failed, then renounced his kingdom and attained liberation on Mount Aṣṭāpada. His emblem is the bull.

deities.earliest_attestation: Historical figure c. 9th–8th c. BCE (traditional); Kalpa Sūtra
deities.summary: The twenty-third Tīrthaṅkara, prince of Vārāṇasī, who saved a pair of snakes burning in an ascetic's fire. In his final meditation the demon Meghamālin (his enemy through many births, Kamaṭha) assailed him with storms, and the serpent king Dharaṇendra with Padmāvatī spread his hood over him. His fourfold restraint preceded Mahāvīra's teaching.

The twenty-second Tīrthaṅkara, cousin of Kṛṣṇa, who on his wedding day heard the cries of animals penned for the feast and renounced the world at once; his bride Rājīmatī followed him into renunciation. He attained liberation on Mount Girnar.

The twenty-four Ford-Makers of each half time-cycle, from Ṛṣabha to Mahāvīra, who conquered passions, attained omniscience and taught the path across the ocean of rebirth. They neither create nor intervene; they are worshipped as perfect models.

deities.earliest_attestation: Shravanabelagola statue 981 CE; Ādipurāṇa (9th c. CE)
deities.summary: Son of Ṛṣabha who defeated his brother Bharata in combat, then renounced the kingdom on the field and stood in meditation so long that vines grew up his limbs. Dig. Jains hold him the first to attain liberation in this cycle; his 17-metre statue at Shravanabelagola is anointed every twelve years (Mahāmastakābhiṣeka).

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 9th–10th c. CE images; Śvetāmbara and Digambara hymns
deities.summary: The yakṣī (śāsanadevī) of Pārśvanātha, queen of Dharaṇendra, who sheltered the Jina with her husband. Crowned with a serpent hood, she is the most worshipped Jain goddess, granting protection and worldly aid to devotees.

The yakṣī of Neminātha, a mother goddess seated under a mango tree with a child on her lap and a lion as mount. Once a devout wife driven from home, she gave her life with her sons and was reborn as the goddess.
The nāga king (yakṣa of Pārśvanātha), reborn from one of the snakes Pārśva saved from the fire, who spread his hoods over the Jina during Meghamālin's assault.

The enemy of Pārśvanātha across ten lifetimes, born as the ascetic Kamaṭha whose fire Pārśva exposed, and as the demon Meghamālin who hurled storms and floods at the meditating Jina. Defeated by his equanimity, he finally converted.

primary_sources: Guru Granth Sahib (Japji and Nanak's hymns)
deities.summary: The first Guru and founder of the Sikh path, who after three days in the river Vein proclaimed 'there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' and taught the remembrance of the One Name (Nām), honest work and sharing. His light passed to each successive Guru and now dwells in the Guru Granth Sahib.

The tenth Guru, poet and warrior, who created the Khalsa at Anandpur on Vaisakhi 1699 with the initiation of the double-edged sword, and before his death declared the Guru Granth Sahib the eternal Guru.

primary_sources: Ardas (Sikh common prayer, opening 'Pritham Bhagauti simar kai')
deities.summary: The divine power as sword: the Ardās begins 'First remembering Bhagautī, then remember Guru Nānak.' In the Dasam Granth's Chaṇḍī dī Vār the goddess Chaṇḍī battles the demons; in Sikh reading Bhagautī is the Timeless One's power that destroys evil.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 11th c. CE (Bön canon); claimed pre-Buddhist
deities.summary: The primordial Buddha of the Bön Dzogchen teachings, naked and blue like the sky, the dharmakāya from which the Bön teachings flow through Shenlha Ökar to Tönpa Shenrab.
The Great Mother of Bön, embodiment of wisdom and love (also Sherab Jamma), one of the four Transcendent Lords; mother of all enlightened beings.
The god of compassion of Bön, one of the four Transcendent Lords, the sambhogakāya who transmits the teachings from Kuntu Zangpo to Tönpa Shenrab.
The fierce Queen of Existence, chief protector of Bön, riding a mule over a sea of blood, with six arms and three faces; also adopted by some Tibetan Buddhist lineages.
The demon prince who opposed Tönpa Shenrab throughout his life, stealing his horses and seeking to destroy his teaching, until at last he was converted and became a disciple.

deities.earliest_attestation: Dunhuang-era Tibetan (8th–10th c. CE) mountain cult references; later rituals
deities.summary: The great mountain deity of the Nyenchen Thanglha range north of Lhasa, a white god on a white horse, ancestor-protector of central Tibet and lord of the nyen spirits; bound by Padmasambhava as a Dharma protector.

primary_sources: Kalasha oral tradition and festival hymns
deities.summary: The creator god of the Kalasha, distant and supreme, who made the world and the other gods; in the related Nuristani religion he corresponds to Imra (Yamrāy), the creator.
A powerful god of the Kalasha, protector of the valley, of crops and herds, and intercessor with the creator; honoured with goat sacrifice at his altar with carved horse heads.
Goddess of the home, family and marriage, whose clan temple (Jestak Han) holds the community's domestic rites.
The heroic god who rides in on a horse from the land of Tsiyam each winter solstice at the Chaumos festival, counts the people, receives their offerings and returns, carrying their prayers.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 17th–18th c. CE (Malla court institution; earlier kumārī-pūjā)
deities.summary: A prepubescent girl of the Newar Shakya caste chosen by strict signs to embody the goddess Taleju until her first menstruation. The Royal Kumārī of Kathmandu blesses the head of state each year at Indra Jātrā.

The tutelary goddess of the Malla kings, a form of Durgā brought from Simraungadh; her temples tower over each Durbar Square, open to the public only at Dasaiñ. She withdrew from playing dice with the king and promised to dwell in a virgin girl — the Kumārī.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 7th c. CE (legend: Narendradeva); chariot festival records from Licchavi/early Malla
deities.summary: The red rain-giving god of Patan, worshipped by Buddhists as Karuṇāmaya Avalokiteśvara and by Hindus as the yogi Matsyendranāth. When Gorakhnāth sat on the rain-serpents and caused a twelve-year drought, he was brought from Kāmarūpa in the form of a bee, and Gorakhnāth rose to greet his guru, releasing the nāgas. His enormous chariot is pulled through Patan each year.
The Pāṇḍava hero Bhīma deified as patron of Newar traders and craftsmen; merchants keep his image in their shops and he is honoured along the old trade routes to Tibet.

Mother goddess of the Turks, protector of women, childbirth, children and the placenta, wife or consort of Tengri. In the Orkhon inscriptions the khagan's mother is compared to her: 'like Umay my mother the Katun'.
The sacred Earth-and-Water, the homeland as a living divine power, invoked with Tengri and Umay in the Orkhon inscriptions as the protector of the Turkic people.

deities.earliest_attestation: 13th c. CE (Plano Carpini, Marco Polo); Mongol ritual
deities.summary: Mother Earth of the Mongols, consort of Tengri (Father Heaven), giver of fertility to herds and people. Marco Polo describes household felt images of the earth-god Natigay with wife and children, fed with meat at meals.

deities.earliest_attestation: 13th c. CE (Plano Carpini on fire purification); Mongol fire prayers
primary_sources: Plano Carpini, History of the Mongols
deities.summary: The mother spirit of the hearth fire (golomt), centre of the ger and lineage; purifier through whose flames visitors and goods passed. Fat is offered to her at the winter fire-sacrifice.

deities.earliest_attestation: 13th–16th c. CE (Mongolian Buddhist and shamanic texts)
deities.summary: Chief of the thirty-three tengri (Buryat: of the fifty-five western, benevolent tengri), father of Geser. His name descends, through Sogdian, from Ahura Mazdā, while Mongolian Buddhism identifies him with Indra-Śakra, king of the Thirty-Three.

primary_sources: Buryat shamanic prayers and Geser epic
deities.summary: Leader of the forty-four eastern, malevolent tengri of the Buryats, whose war against the fifty-five western tengri of Khan Khurmas drives the cosmic drama of the Geser epic; demons cast down from his side became earthly evils.
The Bull Lord, a heavenly being who descended as a bull, fathered the Buryat Ekhirit and Bulagat clans and is honoured as their ancestral master spirit of the Baikal region.

deities.earliest_attestation: Turkic folk tradition (widespread; records 19th c. CE)
primary_sources: Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Tatar folk tradition
deities.summary: A female demon with long hair and pendulous breasts, often with backward feet, who attacks women in childbirth and newborns, strangling them or stealing the mother's liver. Iron, onions and a protecting shaman or mullah drive her away.

Patron-spirit of horses among the Kazakhs, one of the four livestock patrons (with Zengi-baba of cattle, Shopan-ata of sheep, Oisyl-kara of camels); horse-breeders call on him at foaling and in danger.

deities.earliest_attestation: Epic in oral performance (written records 19th c. CE); Manas Ordo, Talas
primary_sources: Epic of Manas (Kyrgyz oral epic; recitations of Sagymbai Orozbakov and Sayakbai Karalaev)
deities.summary: The Kyrgyz epic hero who united the forty tribes and fought the Kalmyks and Chinese; manaschi reciters receive the epic in dreams, and pilgrims visit his ordo at Talas.
The Scythian sky-father whom Herodotus calls 'most rightly named' Zeus, husband of Api the Earth, ancestor of the Scythians through their first man Targitaos.

primary_sources: Herodotus 4.5 (mother of Targitaos as daughter of the Borysthenes)
deities.summary: The Scythian Earth goddess, wife of Papaios, whom Herodotus equates with Gē; possibly also the snake-legged mother of the Scythians in the Greek origin legend.
The god Herodotus equates with Apollo; perhaps a solar or herd-protecting god (name possibly 'rich in pastures').

The goddess Herodotus equates with Heavenly Aphrodite; patron of the Enarees, effeminate diviners who received their gift from her. Gold plaques show a goddess enthroned before a horseman with a rhyton.
The god worshipped by the Royal Scythians, equated by Herodotus with Poseidon — likely a god of waters and horses.

The war god of the Scythians, unnamed by Herodotus, worshipped as an ancient iron sword set on a vast platform of brushwood in each district, to which horses, cattle and every hundredth war captive were sacrificed.

The first man of Scythia, son of Zeus (Papaios) and a daughter of the river Borysthenes. His three sons Lipoxais, Arpoxais and Kolaxais saw golden objects fall from the sky — plough and yoke, axe, cup — which burned the elder two but not the youngest, Kolaxais, who became king.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th–8th c. CE (Sogdian Buddhist texts; Panjikent murals)
deities.summary: The Sogdian wind-god, 'Vayu who works in the upper region', portrayed in Panjikent with three heads, trident and armour; Sogdian Buddhist translations render the Indian Mahādeva (Śiva) as Weshparkar.
The 'great god' of the Sogdians, used in Sogdian Buddhist translations for Indra-Śakra, king of the gods; probably the Sogdian title of the supreme Mazdean god.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The Kushan god shown on coins with four arms, trident, thunderbolt, water-pot, and the bull, in the iconography of Śiva, yet named with the Bactrian descendant of Iranian Vayu, the wind.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1st–3rd c. CE (Kushan coins); Rabatak inscription (Mihir)
primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The Bactrian Mithra, shown on Kushan coins as a radiate solar god with a sword, god of contract, light and kingship.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The Bactrian form of Verethragna, the Iranian god of victory, depicted on Kushan coins as a warrior with a bird-crowned helmet, spear and sword.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The divine royal glory (Avestan khvarenah) personified, shown on Kushan coins as a youth holding fire or a purse; the glory that chooses and leaves kings.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: Goddess of abundance and fortune, Bactrian form of Avestan Aṣ̌i Vaŋuhī ('Good Reward'), shown on coins holding a cornucopia.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The Kushan moon god, shown with a crescent behind his shoulders.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The Kushan fire god, shown with flames rising from his shoulders, the Bactrian form of Avestan Ātar.

primary_sources: Olonkho epics (e.g. Nyurgun Bootur the Swift, recorded by P. A. Oyunsky)
deities.summary: The supreme White Creator Lord dwelling in the ninth heaven, head of the Aiyy, creator of humans and source of light and life; honoured with mare's milk (kumys) at the summer Yhyakh festival.
Goddess of childbirth and fertility who brings the child's soul down from heaven and attends every birth, of humans and of cattle.
The mighty and terrible lord of the western upper-world abaasy, ambivalent master of fate, who gave humanity one of its three souls and fire, and who rules the black shamans.

Lord of the Lower World and chief of the lower abaasy, a monstrous figure with mouth on his forehead who devours souls and sends his demonic sons to wreck the Middle World; enemy of the Olonkho heroes.
The forest spirit and master of game, who gives animals to hunters who respect him; hunters feed the fire for him and never boast of their catch.
The supreme sky-god and creator of the Evenki, who with his rival brother Khargi formed the earth from soil brought up from the primordial waters, and who owns the animals and the upper world.
The evil younger brother of Seveki, master of the lower world, who marred creation with harmful beasts and sends illness through his spirits.
The great hunter-ancestor who chases the cosmic elk Kheglen across the sky (the Milky Way is his ski track) to recover the sun; guardian of the clan's path to the lower world of the dead.
The sky-father of the Mansi and Khanty, dwelling in the highest heaven, who sent down the earth-diver bird to bring up soil and made the earth; father of the World-Surveyor Man and of the bear.

Mother goddess of the Mansi, sister or wife of Num-Torum, who writes each newborn's destiny and length of life in a golden book or on a tree, and attends childbirth; she is linked with the hare and the goose.

The 'World-Watching Man', youngest son of Num-Torum, who rides a white horse round the world watching over humans, carries their prayers to heaven and wins his place by cleverness; also a goose-shaped psychopomp.
The lord of the underworld and of disease-spirits (kul), brother and opponent of Num-Torum, who spoils creation and takes the souls of the dead.
The sky-god and creator of the Nenets, ruler of the upper world and the weather, who sent birds to dive for earth and made the world; reindeer are sacrificed to him at sacred sites.
God of the underworld and of death, who in the creation myth tried to destroy what Num made, and who sends disease; Num had to grant him a share of the world.
Mother Earth of the Nenets, protector of women and childbirth, wife of Num in some accounts; offerings are made to her through the earth.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ethnographic records 19th–20th c. CE (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)
primary_sources: Chukchi myth collections (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)
deities.summary: Raven, the creator-transformer of the Chukchi, who at the Creator's prompting made the earth with his droppings, freed the sun, moon and stars from a container and brought light; a glutton and trickster as well as creator.

primary_sources: Chukchi shamanic tradition (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)
deities.summary: Malevolent spirits of the Chukchi who hunt human souls as people hunt animals, causing illness and death; shamans fight them and protective rites deceive them.

primary_sources: Krasheninnikov, Description of the Land of Kamchatka (1755)
Koryak myth collections (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)
deities.summary: Big Raven of the Koryak and Itelmen, first ancestor and creator-trickster who made Kamchatka, lives with his wife Miti and fools and is fooled in endless tales; the ancestor to whom the Koryak trace their way of life.

facets.core_claim: Dyaus is the bright sky itself and its fatherhood: 'Heaven is my father, my begetter' (RV 1.164.33). Paired with Earth he engenders the world and the gods.
facets.scholarly_note: Dyaus Pitā is the closest linguistic survival of PIE *Dyēus ph2tēr (Greek Zeus Patēr, Latin Iuppiter). His cult in the Rigveda is already faded, an instance of the 'deus otiosus' pattern.

facets.core_claim: 'Earth is my mother, I am her son' (Atharvaveda 12.1.12). She bears all creatures, holds the herbs and waters, and is the firm ground of dharma.
facets.scholarly_note: In Puranic Hinduism she becomes Bhūdevī, consort of Viṣṇu (rescued by Varāha) — continuity of the Vedic figure into Vaiṣṇava theology.

facets.core_claim: Savitṛ, golden-handed and golden-eyed, raises his arms and sets the world in motion and in rest; even the waters and winds keep his ordinances.
facets.scholarly_note: Often distinguished from Sūrya as the sun's animating power rather than its disk; the distinction blurs in later Vedic texts.

facets.facet_name: Guide of Roads and of the Dead
facets.core_claim: Pūṣan knows every road; he protects herds, brings back what is lost, conducts brides to their new home and leads the departed safely to the fathers (RV 10.17).
Aryaman keeps the customs that bind the people: guest-friendship, the marriage alliance and the safety of roads; he leads the ancestors.
facets.scholarly_note: Dumézil's Mitra-Varuna places Aryaman as a minor sovereign alongside Mitra (contract) and Varuṇa (binding power); an Avestan cognate Airyaman exists.

facets.core_claim: Bhaga deals out to each his lot of wealth and luck; 'even the strong man says: may I share in Bhaga' (RV 7.41.2).
facets.scholarly_note: Cognate with Avestan baga and Old Persian baga 'god', and Slavic bogŭ 'god' (via Iranian); the word for 'god' in several languages derives from the same 'allotter' root.

facets.core_claim: Parjanya roars like a lion, strikes down the trees and the wicked, and pours the waters that make the whole earth fruitful (RV 5.83).
facets.scholarly_note: A connection to PIE *Perkʷunos (Lithuanian Perkūnas, Slavic Perun) has been proposed but is phonologically contested.

facets.core_claim: Prajāpati emits the creatures from his own body and is emptied by it; the sacrificer rebuilds him in the agnicayana altar, renewing the cosmos (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa).
facets.scholarly_note: Brāhmaṇa theology; Prajāpati's role passes to Brahmā in classical Hinduism. The question-verse refrain of RV 10.121 ('to which god shall we offer?') was later read as naming the god 'Ka'.

facets.facet_name: The Golden Embryo on the Waters
facets.core_claim: 'In the beginning arose the Golden Embryo; once born, he was the one lord of creation; he held the earth and this sky' (RV 10.121.1). From the egg the whole cosmos unfolds.
Trita, urged by Indra, kills the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ and recovers the cows (RV 10.8.8). He bears the guilt of the slaying for the gods.
facets.scholarly_note: Cognate with Avestan Thrita / Thraētaona (slayer of three-headed Aži Dahāka) and the reconstructed PIE *Tritós who kills a three-headed serpent to regain cattle.

facets.core_claim: Apām Napāt blazes in the waters without kindling; the young waters circle and bathe him, and he gives the world its being (RV 2.35).
facets.scholarly_note: Shared Indo-Iranian deity (Avestan Apąm Napāt, guardian of the khvarenah in the sea Vourukasha). A cognate with Irish Nechtan and Roman Neptunus has been proposed and is debated.

facets.facet_name: The Rock Withholding the Cows of Light
facets.core_claim: Vala encloses the cows — the dawns and the light — in the mountain; the sacred song breaks him open and the day returns.
facets.scholarly_note: The Vala myth is a doublet of the Vṛtra myth: one withholds waters, the other light/cattle; both are opened by Indra.

facets.core_claim: Rudra the red, the wild archer whose arrows bring sickness to man and beast, is begged to turn his weapon away; the same Rudra holds a thousand remedies and is the best of physicians (RV 2.33).
facets.scholarly_note: Rudra is the Vedic precursor of Śiva, whose name 'auspicious' was first a euphemistic epithet of Rudra (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad).

facets.core_claim: The Aśvins drive their honey-chariot ahead of Dawn; they rescue the shipwrecked, restore sight and youth, and give a lost leg of iron to Viśpalā (RV 1.116–117).
facets.scholarly_note: The Aśvins, the Greek Dioskouroi and the Lithuanian Dievo sūneliai ('sons of god') are the standard PIE 'divine twins' set; Mitanni treaty names them as Nāsatya.

facets.core_claim: The Maruts, sons of Rudra and Pṛśni, ride with spears of lightning and golden ornaments, shake mountains, and fight beside Indra against Vṛtra.

Viśvakarman, with eyes, mouths, arms and feet on every side, welds heaven and earth together; he is the father who offered all worlds in sacrifice (RV 10.81–82). In the Purāṇas he builds the cities and weapons of the gods.
facets.scholarly_note: Vedic Viśvakarman is a cosmogonic creator; Puranic Viśvakarman is the divine architect, often merged with Tvaṣṭṛ.

facets.core_claim: Tvaṣṭṛ forges Indra's vajra, shapes every form in the womb and fashions the cup of the gods; his three-headed son Viśvarūpa and his creature Vṛtra oppose Indra.
Kāma, with his sugar-cane bow and flower arrows, pierces gods and men; when he shot Śiva the god's third eye burned him to ash, yet he lives on bodiless (Anaṅga) in every heart.
facets.scholarly_note: In RV 10.129 kāma (desire) is 'the first seed of mind' at the beginning — the cosmogonic root of the later deity.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Wealth and the Yakṣas
facets.core_claim: Kubera, king of the yakṣas, keeper of the treasures of the earth, rules Alakā on Kailāsa and guards the north.
Proud of his boon, Mahiṣa seizes Indra's throne; only a woman — the Devī formed from all the gods' energies — can and does slay him.
facets.scholarly_note: Mysore (Mahishuru) claims him as its eponym; some Adivasi and Dalit communities (e.g. Asur people) honour Mahishasura as an ancestor king.

facets.core_claim: Hiraṇyakaśipu declares himself the only god and demands his son worship him; his perfect boon is undone by a god who is neither man nor beast.
Hiraṇyākṣa hides the Earth under the waters of dissolution; Varāha kills him and raises her back to her place.
Mahābali's reign was a golden age; dethroned by Vāmana, he is honoured for keeping his promise and returns every Onam.
facets.scholarly_note: Kerala tradition portrays Mahabali as beloved; some political readings treat the Vamana story as Brahmanical displacement of a local king.

facets.core_claim: Balarāma bears the plough and pestle, drinks and fights with unmatched strength; at his death a white serpent leaves his mouth — he was Śeṣa all along.
facets.scholarly_note: One of the earliest attested Vaiṣṇava figures: depicted with plough on Indo-Greek coins of Agathocles beside Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Universe at Puri
facets.core_claim: Jagannātha is Kṛṣṇa-Viṣṇu himself, present in the dāru-brahman (wooden absolute); his prasāda erases caste distinctions among those who share it.
facets.scholarly_note: Many scholars see a tribal (Sabara) origin for the wooden icons; the temple legend preserves this in the story of Viśvavasu the Sabara.

facets.facet_name: The God Who Waits on the Brick
facets.core_claim: Viṭṭhala waits on the brick for his devotees; he is mother and father to the poor saints of the Vārkarī path.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Seven Hills for the Kali Age
facets.core_claim: Veṅkaṭeśvara dwells on the Seven Hills to save humanity in the Kali Yuga; whoever surrenders at his feet is protected.
Ayyappan unites Śiva and Viṣṇu in one son; whoever keeps the vow and calls 'Swamiye Saranam Ayyappa' becomes Ayyappa — devotee and deity share his name.
facets.scholarly_note: Ayyappan is widely linked with the older Sāstā / Ayyanār guardian cult of Tamil and Kerala villages.

facets.core_claim: Khaṇḍobā rides out on his horse with sword and dog to destroy Maṇi and Malla and protect his devotees; he is the family god (kuladevata) of Maharashtrian households of every caste.
facets.scholarly_note: Likely a regional pastoral deity Sanskritized as a form of Śiva/Bhairava.

facets.core_claim: Sūrya, soul of all that moves and stands (RV 1.115.1), sees all deeds, drives away darkness and disease, and is the visible form of Brahman.
facets.scholarly_note: Saura iconography (boots, tunic) and the Maga priests of the Sāmba Purāṇa reflect Iranian influence on North Indian sun worship.

facets.core_claim: Candra is the cup of soma drunk by the gods each fortnight and refilled; he governs mind, plants and the lunar mansions.
Maṅgala, the fiery son of Bhūmi, grants courage and land, and when ill-placed brings strife and accidents.
Bṛhaspati is the power of prayer (brahman) itself, priest of the devas, whose song broke open the rock and freed the light.
Śukra, the one-eyed sage, alone knows the secret of raising the slain; he serves the asuras with perfect loyalty, warning Bali against Vāmana.
Śani dispenses the fruit of one's deeds without favour; his affliction purifies, and those who endure it rise.
facets.scholarly_note: Indian astrology absorbed Hellenistic planetary lore (Yavanajātaka, 2nd–3rd c. CE); Śani's malefic character matches Hellenistic Saturn.

facets.core_claim: Rāhu the head, immortal but bodiless, chases the sun and moon; at every eclipse he devours them, and they slip out through his severed throat.
Ketu, the body without a head, cuts attachments and grants mokṣa-oriented insight, even as he brings sudden loss.
The grahas take hold of every life according to karma; worship of all nine together averts their harm.
Gaṅgā flows from Viṣṇu's foot through Śiva's locks to earth and on to the underworld; she washes away sin and carries the dead to liberation.
Śeṣa remains when all else dissolves; on his coils Viṣṇu rests between creations, and his yawning shakes the earth.

facets.facet_name: Rope of the Churning of the Ocean
facets.core_claim: Vāsuki gives his body as the rope of the cosmic churning, enduring both sides' pulling so that the nectar of immortality appears.

facets.facet_name: Serpent Guardians of Waters and Treasure
facets.core_claim: The nāgas hold the rains and springs and the hidden jewels of the earth; honoured, they give fertility and offspring; offended, they bring drought and skin disease.
Garuḍa, blazing like fire, defeats the gods, takes the amṛta yet does not drink it, and wins his mother's freedom; Viṣṇu makes him his vehicle and banner.
facets.scholarly_note: Garuda spread across Buddhist Asia (garuḍa/khyung, Indonesian national emblem, Thai royal insignia).

facets.core_claim: Sītā comes from the furrow and returns to the earth's embrace; her steadfastness is the measure of dharma.
facets.scholarly_note: The Vedic Sītā is the personified furrow (RV 4.57); the epic heroine preserves the agrarian origin.

facets.core_claim: Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa are one soul in two bodies; she is the inner power of God's own joy, and pure love (prema) flows from her.
Nārada moves freely among gods, demons and men, carrying news and kindling conflicts that bring the plan of Viṣṇu to fruition.

facets.facet_name: The Guru Who Is the Trinity
facets.core_claim: Dattātreya is the original guru, the three gods in one form, who teaches non-duality to all who seek, free of caste and rule.

facets.facet_name: Queen of Serpents Who Demands Worship
facets.core_claim: Manasā both sends and cures snakebite; those who refuse her suffer, those who honour her are protected and blessed with children.

facets.facet_name: Goddess Who Brings and Cools the Pox
facets.core_claim: Śītalā's visitation is the fever; her grace is its cooling. She sweeps disease away with her broom and sprinkles healing water.
Dhanvantari came up from the milk ocean with the nectar of immortality and taught the science of life to humanity.

facets.facet_name: Skull-Bearing Guardian of the Sacred City
facets.core_claim: Bhairava punishes pride, guards every temple's boundary and the city of Kāśī; even death (Kāla) fears him.
facets.scholarly_note: Bhairava's skull-penance myth reflects Kāpālika ascetic practice; in Kashmir Śaivism Bhairava names the supreme consciousness itself.

facets.core_claim: Vīrabhadra is Śiva's grief turned to fury; he shatters the rite that excluded Śiva and restores the god's due.
Nandī is the perfect devotee who forever gazes at Śiva; through him the worshipper approaches the Lord.
Each god's power takes female form and rides his mount into battle; together with Kālī they annihilate Raktabīja.
facets.scholarly_note: The epic Mothers of Skanda are dangerous child-seizing beings; the later Seven Mothers are protective goddesses — a transformation visible in iconography.

facets.facet_name: Ten Faces of the Goddess in Ten Directions
facets.core_claim: The Mahāvidyās are the full spectrum of the Goddess, from terrible to beautiful; each is a path of wisdom, and together they are the one Mahādevī.

facets.facet_name: Goddess Whose Body Became the Sacred Land
facets.core_claim: Satī's sacrifice consecrates the land: every Śakti Pīṭha holds a part of her body, and the Goddess is present in the earth itself.
Kāmākhyā is the creative womb of the cosmos; her monthly cycle renews the fertility of the earth.
Ayyanār circles the village boundary on horseback through the night; no evil spirit or thief passes him.
facets.scholarly_note: Identified with Ayyappan as Sāstā (Hariharaputra); worship is often vegetarian at his shrine while his attendants (e.g. Karuppasamy) receive animal sacrifice.

facets.core_claim: Māri is the heat that brings the pustules and the rain that cools them; her devotees honour her with neem leaves and cool offerings so that she may be gentle.
facets.scholarly_note: One Tamil origin legend identifies her with Renukā (Yellamma), whose head was joined to an outcaste woman's body.

facets.core_claim: Renukā was slain for a moment's doubt and raised again; she now mothers the poor and outcast who come to her hill.
facets.scholarly_note: The devadasi dedication once associated with her cult was outlawed by the Karnataka Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act, 1982.

facets.core_claim: Munīśvaran drives off demons and malevolent ghosts; once satisfied he guards his people faithfully.
Karuppu stands at the eighteen steps and judges disputes; a false oath sworn before his sickle brings ruin.

facets.facet_name: Final Avatar Who Ends the Kali Age
facets.core_claim: Nārāyaṇa came as Vaikuṇḍar to destroy the last fragment of Kroni and inaugurate the age of Dharma; all castes drink from one well before him.
facets.scholarly_note: Historically a 19th-c. social-religious reform movement against caste oppression in Travancore.

facets.facet_name: Primordial Evil Reborn in Every Age
facets.core_claim: Kroni was divided and each piece took birth to fight the avatāras; with the destruction of Kaliyan, evil ends forever.
'The rich will make temples for Śiva; what shall I, a poor man, do? My legs are pillars, the body the shrine, the head a cupola of gold' (Basava).
Basava taught that work is worship (kāyakave kailāsa) and that every devotee of Śiva is equal; in him Nandī came to earth.
facets.scholarly_note: Venerated rather than worshipped in most Lingayat practice; included as the tradition's founding figure.

facets.core_claim: In the beginning was only water and Phura; from his breath came the gods and from his will the world.

facets.facet_name: King of Heaven, Ancestor of Kings
facets.core_claim: Lengdon rules heaven and gave the Ahom their kings; the Swargadeo is heaven's descendant.
facets.scholarly_note: Assamese Hinduization identified Lengdon with Indra.

facets.facet_name: Divine Brothers Who Descended to Rule
facets.core_claim: The brothers came down the golden ladder with the sacred Somdeo image and taught the worship of ancestors.
Vajrapāṇi wields the vajra of indestructible wisdom; he protects the Buddha and the Dharma and is the power aspect of the enlightened mind, with Mañjuśrī (wisdom) and Avalokiteśvara (compassion).
facets.scholarly_note: In Gandharan art Vajrapāṇi is depicted with the iconography of Herakles (club-like vajra, lion skin) — a documented Greco-Buddhist adaptation.

facets.core_claim: The Four Great Kings report to Śakra on the deeds of humans and protect all who uphold the Dharma; the Āṭānāṭiya protective verses are their gift.
Vaiśravaṇa, who 'hears everything', guards the north, rules the yakṣas and grants prosperity to those who keep the precepts.
Sakka rules the Tāvatiṃsa heaven by seven vows of virtue; though king of gods, he is a disciple of the Buddha, still within saṃsāra.
facets.scholarly_note: A deliberate reframing of Vedic Indra: powerful but subordinate to the Buddha.

facets.facet_name: Brahmā Who Begged the Buddha to Teach
facets.core_claim: Sahampati kneels before the Buddha and requests the turning of the Wheel; the highest god of the world becomes the Dharma's first petitioner.
facets.scholarly_note: The Brahmajāla's deluded Brahmā, who mistakes being first-born for being creator, is a Buddhist critique of Brahmanical creator theology.

facets.core_claim: Hārītī, once the terror of mothers, learned compassion through her own loss; now she guards children and grants offspring, and the monasteries feed her each day.
facets.scholarly_note: Often paired with the yakṣa Pāñcika; Gandharan Hārītī with cornucopia shares iconography with Kushan Ardochsho and Greek Tyche.

facets.facet_name: Tamer of the Spirits of Tibet
facets.core_claim: Guru Rinpoche, born in a lotus, subdued the gods and demons of the land and made them guardians of the Dharma; he will return to all who call him.
facets.scholarly_note: Historical role is uncertain; the Testament of Ba records an 8th-c. tantric master; the larger biography develops in terma literature.

facets.core_claim: Pehar was once a wild king of spirits; bound by oath he now protects the Dharma and the Tibetan government and prophesies through his medium.
Gesar was a son of heaven born among men; he defeated the demons of north, south, east and west and will return to lead the armies of Shambhala.
facets.scholarly_note: In Buryat and Mongolian versions (Abai Geser) he is the son of Khormusta Tengri — a bridge between Tibetan and Mongol religion.

facets.core_claim: Whoever hears the name of Bhaiṣajyaguru is freed from disease, misfortune and rebirth in the lower realms; his blue light heals all ills.

facets.facet_name: Wisdom That Gives Birth to Buddhas
facets.core_claim: 'The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of the Buddhas' (Aṣṭasāhasrikā): all awakened ones are born from the realization of emptiness she embodies.
The five Jinas are the enlightened nature of the five aggregates; anger becomes mirror-wisdom, pride equality, desire discernment, envy accomplishment, ignorance the Dharmadhātu.
facets.scholarly_note: The Western term 'Dhyāni Buddha' was popularized by Brian Hodgson in the 19th c.; Sanskrit sources call them Jinas or Tathāgatas.

facets.core_claim: Mucalinda shelters the Awakened One from cold and rain; the serpent power of the waters becomes the Dharma's protector.

facets.facet_name: First Ford-Maker and Teacher of Civilization
facets.core_claim: Ṛṣabha first gave humanity its arts and laws, then showed the path beyond them; he is the first of the twenty-four who cross and help others cross.
facets.scholarly_note: Also honoured in Hindu tradition as a partial avatāra of Viṣṇu (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5).

facets.core_claim: Pārśva remained unshaken under the storms of hatred; liberated on Sammeda Śikhara, he shows that equanimity conquers enmity across lifetimes.
facets.scholarly_note: Widely regarded as the earliest Jina with probable historicity.

facets.facet_name: Renouncer Moved by the Animals' Cries
facets.core_claim: Nemi turned back from his own wedding for the sake of animals; compassion for every living being is the door to liberation.
Each Tīrthaṅkara builds a ford across saṃsāra by founding the fourfold community; venerating them purifies the soul by contemplation, not by their intervention.
Victorious, Bāhubali saw the emptiness of victory; standing immovable in kāyotsarga, he conquered himself.
Padmāvatī guards the teaching of Pārśva and answers the prayers of the faithful who honour the Jina.
facets.scholarly_note: Jain doctrine holds that liberated Jinas do not respond to petitions; worldly requests go to guardian deities such as Padmāvatī.

facets.core_claim: Ambikā protects children and the faithful of Nemi's teaching; her mango tree bears fruit for those who honour the Jina.

facets.facet_name: Grateful Serpent King Who Shielded the Jina
facets.core_claim: Saved by Pārśva in a previous life, Dharaṇendra repaid him by sheltering him in his supreme trial.
Kamaṭha's hatred pursued Pārśva birth after birth, yet could not move him; at last the enemy bowed before the Jina.
Through Nānak the Formless One spoke the Shabad; the same jot (light) passed through the ten Gurus as one flame lights another.
facets.scholarly_note: Sikhs do not regard the Gurus as God incarnate; the Guru is the vessel of the divine Word.

facets.core_claim: The Guru called for heads and created the Pure Ones; the Khalsa is the Guru's own form, sovereign and fearless, protecting the oppressed.
Bhagautī is Akāl's own might, the sword (kirpān) that upholds justice; to remember her is to remember the strength of God.
facets.scholarly_note: Sikh interpretation is contested: some read Bhagautī as the goddess Durgā, the Khalsa mainstream as an attribute of Akal Purakh.

facets.core_claim: Kuntu Zangpo is the pure, empty, luminous nature of mind; all beings are him who have not recognized themselves.
Satrig Ersang is the space of wisdom from which the enlightened arise; she loves all beings as a mother loves her only child.
Shenlha Ökar radiates white light to all beings and is the intermediary between the primordial ground and the teacher in the world.
Sipe Gyalmo rules over all existence and guards the Bön teaching; she destroys its enemies and protects practitioners.
Khyabpa Lagring set every obstacle before Shenrab, yet the Teacher's patience turned him; even the enemy found refuge.
facets.scholarly_note: Structural counterpart of Māra in the Buddha's life story.

facets.core_claim: Thanglha rules the snow peaks and the lake Namtso his consort; he protects the land and the lineages that honour him.
Dezau made all things and stands above the gods who are worshipped at the shrines; the world rests on his creation.
facets.scholarly_note: Nuristani Imra is often derived from Yama-rājan, linking him to Vedic Yama; Kalasha usage of Khodai reflects Persian/Islamic influence.

facets.core_claim: Mahandeo guards the valley's fields and flocks and carries the people's petitions to Dezau.
facets.scholarly_note: The name is cognate with Mahādeva (Śiva), but his cult is independent of Hindu Śaivism.

facets.core_claim: Jestak watches over households, marriages and children; her house is the heart of each lineage.
At Chaumos Balumain comes riding from the mythical homeland, blesses the purified people and departs bearing their wishes.
In the chosen Kumārī the goddess Taleju lives visibly; her tika and her gaze confer sovereignty and blessing.
Taleju protects the kingdom and the king who honours her; when he failed her, she chose to live among the people in the Kumārī.
Bunga Dyah brings the monsoon to the valley; his chariot's journey ensures the rains and the rice harvest.
Bhīmsen, strongest of men, guards the trader's road and the shopkeeper's scales.

facets.facet_name: Mother Protector of Birth and Children
facets.core_claim: Umay sits by the cradle and the birthing woman; she brings the child's soul and guards it while it is small.
Tengri above and the holy Yer-Sub below gave the Turks their realm; to betray the land is to offend the sacred.
Under Möngke Tengri, Etügen Eke nourishes grass, herds and children; she is honoured with milk sprinkled to the ground.
The hearth fire is the lineage's life; Mother Fire purifies, protects and must never be insulted by water, blade or filth.
Khormusta leads the western tengri against the dark eastern ones and sends his son Geser to earth to cleanse it of demons.
facets.scholarly_note: A rare documented chain: Avestan Ahura Mazdā → Sogdian Xurmazta → Uyghur/Mongolian Qormusta, with Buddhist identification as Indra.

facets.facet_name: Leader of the Dark Eastern Tengri
facets.core_claim: Ata Ulan and the eastern tengri send sickness and calamity; the shaman appeases them and Geser fights the demons they spawned.
Bukha Noyon came from heaven as a grey bull, defeated the rival bull and became father of the Buryat clans.
Albasty lurks by the birthing woman to steal her lungs or liver and harm the child; she flees from iron and the name of God.
facets.scholarly_note: Cognate figures (Al, Ał) occur in Armenian and Persian folk belief.

facets.core_claim: Kambar-ata keeps the herds of horses; he is called on when mares foal and when the herd is lost in a storm.
Manas, born with blood clots in his hands, gathered the scattered Kyrgyz and guards them still; his spirit inspires the manaschi.
Papaios, father of all, with Api the Earth begot the first Scythian; he is the sky over the steppe.
facets.scholarly_note: The name probably means 'Father' (cf. Greek pappas); Herodotus' equation with Zeus is interpretatio graeca.

facets.core_claim: Api, Earth and Waters, is the mother of the Scythian race and wife of the Sky.
facets.scholarly_note: Name often linked to Iranian *āp- 'water'; the snake-legged goddess of Herodotus 4.9 may be the same figure.

facets.core_claim: Goitosyros brings the light and prosperity of the pastures.
facets.scholarly_note: Interpretation uncertain; known only from Herodotus.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of Divination and Royal Investiture
facets.core_claim: Argimpasa grants sovereignty to the king who drinks from her cup and gives prophecy to her Enarees.
Thagimasadas rules the waters and the horses on which the Royal Scythians ride.
The god lives in the akinakes sword on the brushwood mound; the blood of captives poured over it wins victory.

facets.facet_name: First Ancestor and the Golden Gifts
facets.core_claim: From Targitaos came the Scythians; the heaven-sent golden gifts chose his youngest son as king, and the kings guard them still.
facets.scholarly_note: Dumézil read the four golden objects as the Indo-European three functions (sovereignty/cult, war, production).

facets.core_claim: Weshparkar is the wind that moves through heaven, mighty in battle and in the breath of life.

facets.facet_name: The Great God, King of Gods
facets.core_claim: Adbag is the great god who rules the gods of heaven.
facets.scholarly_note: The equation set Brahmā = Zurvan (Zrwa), Indra = Adbag, Mahādeva = Weshparkar is attested in Sogdian Buddhist texts.

facets.core_claim: Nana, the Lady, rides her lion holding sun and moon; she is the great goddess of the Sogdian cities and of the Kushan kings.
facets.scholarly_note: Descends from the Mesopotamian goddess Nanaya, identified with Inanna/Ishtar; worshipped from Bactria to Panjikent and named in the Rabatak inscription of Kanishka.

facets.core_claim: Oesho, mighty wind of heaven, bearer of trident and bull, protects the Kushan king who stamps his image on coin.
facets.scholarly_note: Whether Oesho is Śiva under a Bactrian name or Vayu in Śiva's iconography is debated; the Sogdian Weshparkar = Mahādeva equation supports a convergence.

facets.core_claim: Miiro, radiant lord of the covenant, watches over oaths and kings.
Orlagno, Smiter of Resistance, brings victory to the righteous king and shatters his enemies.
facets.scholarly_note: Avestan Verethragna 'smiting of resistance/vṛtra' is cognate with Vedic vṛtrahan, Indra's chief epithet 'slayer of Vṛtra'.

facets.core_claim: Pharro is the shining glory that rests on the rightful king; without it no throne endures.

facets.facet_name: Lady of Abundance with the Cornucopia
facets.core_claim: Ardochsho pours out reward and plenty on the righteous and on the realm.
Mao measures the months and lights the night.
facets.scholarly_note: From Iranian Māh 'moon' (Avestan Māh), cognate with Sanskrit mās.

facets.core_claim: Athsho is the holy fire that purifies and carries worship upward.

facets.facet_name: White Creator of the Ninth Heaven
facets.core_claim: Ürüng Aiyy Toyon gives light, warmth and the human soul; at Yhyakh the people greet his sun with kumys.
Aiyysyt descends to the birthing woman bearing the new soul from the upper world; she is thanked with a feast after the birth.

facets.facet_name: Terrible Lord of the Upper West
facets.core_claim: Ulu Toyon, quick to anger, sends disease and death but also gave humans their breath-soul and fire; the shaman must bargain with him.
Arsan Duolai rules the dark lower world, feeding on souls; the heroes of the Middle World must defeat his sons.
Bayanay owns the beasts of the taiga; a hunter's luck is his gift, withdrawn from the greedy and the boastful.
Seveki shaped the earth on the waters and made people and reindeer; Khargi spoiled what he could, but Seveki's work stands.
Whatever Seveki made good, Khargi twisted; mosquitoes, disease and death are his share of creation.

facets.facet_name: Cosmic Hunter Who Recovers the Sun
facets.core_claim: When Kheglen the elk carried the sun into the forest, Mangi pursued it on skis and brought back the day; he watches the road of the dead.
Num-Torum made the earth grow from the mud the loon brought up, lowered the first people, and sent his son to watch over them.

facets.facet_name: Mother Who Writes the Fate of the Newborn
facets.core_claim: Kaltash decides at birth how long each life will last, and protects the mother and child.
Mir-Susne-Khum circles the earth on his winged white horse, seeing all; he intercedes for people and protects them from evil spirits.
Kul-Otyr rules the dark lower world in the north and sends the spirits of sickness; the dead go down to him.
Num sees all from the upper sky, gives warmth and good weather, and made the earth from what the loon brought up.
Nga, master of the lower world, claims the dead and tears at creation; shamans bargain with him for the sick.
Ya-Nebya bears all that lives on the tundra and helps women in childbirth.
Raven flew over the waters and made land, pecked open the dark to free the light, and taught people how to live.
The kelet stalk people as prey; disease is their bite, and the shaman must drive them off.
Kutkh made the land, gave the people fire and sea-creatures, and is their grandfather; his foolishness and cunning both shaped the world.

basis: Sanskrit Dyaus Pitā continues PIE *dyēus ph2tēr phonologically and morphologically
Both are the bright day-sky addressed as 'father'
Both form a sky-father/earth-mother pair (Dyāvāpṛthivī)
Dyaus Pitā and Zeus Patēr (Latin Iuppiter) are exact cognate formulas from *dyēus ph2tēr
Both are sky-fathers of gods and men
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Cognates, not the same cult: Dyaus is nearly inactive in Vedic worship while Zeus is the ruling king of Olympus.

basis: Herodotus explicitly names Papaios as the Scythian Zeus
Both are sky-fathers paired with Earth
Both are ancestors of the royal line (Targitaos son of Zeus)
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Herodotus' equation is interpretatio graeca; Scythian theology is known only through Greek eyes.

basis: Herodotus equates Api with Gē
Both are Earth-mothers wedded to Sky
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Interpretatio graeca in Herodotus 4.59.

basis: Both are the personified Earth, universal mother
Both are paired with Sky (Dyaus / Ouranos) as primordial parents
Earth-mothers paired with a sky-father in neighbouring Indo-Iranian traditions
Both mothers of the people's ancestors
Vedic Mitra and Bactrian Miiro/Iranian Mithra continue one Indo-Iranian god *Mitra, 'contract, alliance'
Both guard oaths and covenants
Both are linked with the sun and light
primary_text_evidence: Mitanni–Hittite treaty of Šattiwaza (c. 1380 BCE) invoking Mi-it-ra with Uruwana, Indara and the Nasatya
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Same inherited deity, developed differently: Vedic Mitra is a quiet companion of Varuṇa, Iranian Mithra a mighty warrior-judge of contract.

basis: Roman Mithras bears the Iranian god's name and Persian dress
Both are solar, invincible, and lords of oath/loyalty
Roman sources themselves call the cult Persian
primary_text_evidence: Plutarch, Life of Pompey 24 (Mithraic rites of the Cilician pirates)
parallels.scholarly_caveat: How much of the Roman mysteries continues Iranian Mithra worship is debated; the tauroctony and grade system have no Iranian counterpart and may be Roman innovations under a Persian name.

basis: Avestan Verethragna (Bactrian Orlagno) = Vedic vṛtrahán 'slayer of Vṛtra/resistance', Indra's chief epithet
Both embody victory over an obstructing foe
parallels.scholarly_caveat: In Zoroastrianism Indra himself is demonized (Vendidad 10.9) while his epithet became an independent yazata — a split of one Indo-Iranian complex.

basis: Sanskrit agní, Latin ignis, Lithuanian ugnis and Old Church Slavonic ognĭ share one root
Both are the sacrificial fire as divine messenger
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Latin ignis is a cognate common noun, not a Roman deity; Roman cult fire was Vesta.

basis: Vedic Yama, Avestan Yima and Old Norse Ymir are cognate with *Yemo 'twin'
Yama is the first mortal who found the path to the realm of the dead
Both are the sacred fire personified as a god carrying worship
Ātar and Agni are parallel Indo-Iranian fire deities
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Names are not cognate (Ātar vs agni); the parallel is functional.

basis: Sogdian Wēšparkar continues Avestan Vayu uparō.kairya 'Vayu working in the upper region'
Avestan Vayu is cognate with Vedic Vāyu, wind and breath
Bactrian Oesho (Wēš) and Sogdian Wēšparkar are the same East Iranian wind god
Both are depicted with Śiva's attributes (trident, multiple heads/arms)
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Some read Oesho as simply Śiva under a Bactrian epithet; the Vayu etymology is widely but not universally accepted.

basis: Oesho is shown with trident, bull, water-pot and multiple arms — standard Śaiva iconography
Kushan kings (Vima Kadphises) styled themselves devotees of Maheśvara
primary_text_evidence: Coins of Vima Kadphises and Vasudeva I

basis: Sogdian Buddhist translators render Mahādeva (Śiva) as Weshparkar
Panjikent images of Weshparkar use Śiva's three heads and trident
parallels.scholarly_caveat: An identification by translation and iconography; the two gods have distinct origins.

basis: Sogdian Buddhist texts translate Indra-Śakra as Adbag
Both are king of the gods of heaven
Sogdian Buddhist translators render Brahmā as Zurvan (Zrwa)
Both are the eldest, highest god of a pantheon
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Translation equivalence chosen by Sogdian Buddhists, not a claim of common origin.

basis: Mongolian Qormusta derives from Sogdian Xurmazta, from Avestan Ahura Mazdā
Both head the benevolent heavenly host against a dark host
parallels.scholarly_caveat: The name traveled; the Mongolian figure is a chief sky-god, not the sole creator of Zoroastrian theology.

basis: Mongolian Buddhism identifies Qormusta with Indra-Śakra
Both rule a heaven of thirty-three gods
primary_text_evidence: Mongolian Buddhist translations of Indra as Qormusta

basis: Sakka is 'Śakra lord of the devas', Indra's Vedic epithet śakra 'mighty'
Both rule the Heaven of the Thirty-Three on Meru
Buddhism keeps Indra's kingship but makes him a disciple
Buddhist Mahābrahmā is the Brahmanical creator Brahmā
The Brahmajāla Sutta reframes his creator claim as a delusion of being first-born
Thai Phra Phrom is Brahmā as received through Theravāda and Brahmanical court ritual
Both four-faced high gods subordinate to the Buddha
Vaiśravaṇa ('son of Viśravas') is Kubera's patronymic
Both rule the yakṣas, guard the north and give wealth
parallels.source_tradition: Buddhist adoption of the Brahmanical Kubera

basis: Buddhist Yama Dharmarāja is the Vedic-Hindu Yama adopted as judge of the hells
Both judge the dead according to their deeds
Mahākāla 'Great Black/Time' is a name of Śiva
Buddhist Mahākāla keeps Śaiva features: third eye, skull ornaments, trident, cremation ground
Buddhist narratives tell of Śiva subdued and made protector
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Tibetan tradition regards Mahākāla as a wrathful emanation of Avalokiteśvara, not as Śiva; the derivation is historical, not doctrinal.

basis: Guanyin translates Avalokiteśvara ('Perceiver of the World's Sounds')
Both answer every call for help (Lotus Sūtra ch. 25)
The figure was feminized in China from about the 10th–12th c.
Newar Buddhists worship Bunga Dyah as Karuṇāmaya Avalokiteśvara
Both compassionate saviours who relieve suffering — here drought
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Hindus identify the same image with the Nāth yogi Matsyendranāth — a double identity typical of Kathmandu Valley religion.

basis: Gandharan reliefs depict Vajrapāṇi with Herakles' club-form vajra, lion skin and muscular nudity
Both are invincible divine protectors
parallels.scholarly_caveat: An artistic borrowing in Greco-Buddhist Gandhara, not a theological identification.

basis: Vajrapāṇi 'vajra-in-hand' is also Indra's epithet
Both wield the thunderbolt as protector-warriors
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Buddhist texts sometimes conflate Vajrapāṇi with Śakra; later Vajrayāna makes them distinct.

basis: Bhairava is the terrible form emanated by Śiva himself
Same skull, dog and cremation-ground attributes
Bactrian/Sogdian Nana descends from Mesopotamian Nanaya, long syncretized with Inanna/Ishtar
Both are lion-associated queens of heaven bearing sun/moon or star symbols
The cult spread east via Achaemenid and Seleucid networks
parallels.scholarly_caveat: The source goddess is Nanaya, distinct from Inanna in early Sumer though identified with Ishtar from the 2nd millennium BCE.

basis: Both are goddesses enthroned on or riding a lion
Both are sovereign, martial great goddesses
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Direct influence of Nana's lion iconography on Durgā's has been proposed but is unproven.

basis: Vedic Rudra is the same god later called Śiva
Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad already names Rudra as Śiva the supreme
Both are archers whose arrows bring plague
Both are also healers who withhold the arrow when appeased
Viśvakarman offers all worlds in sacrifice (RV 10.81)
Puruṣa is sacrificed to form the world (RV 10.90)
Both hymns make cosmogony a sacrifice
Both are divine craftsmen-architects of the gods' dwellings and weapons
Both forge the storm-king's weapon and the gods' vessels
Both are artisans whose offspring cause trouble
Both are benevolent divine twins who bring healing/growth to humans
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Typological only; no historical link between Vedic and Haudenosaunee twins.

basis: RV 10.121's refrain resolves in its last verse: 'Prajāpati, no one but you encompasses all these'
Both are the one lord of creation at the beginning
Manusmṛti and the Purāṇas: Brahmā is born within the golden egg on the waters
The Vedic golden embryo becomes the classical creator's birth
Both cosmogonies begin with a cosmic egg from which the first being emerges
Both separate heaven and earth from the egg
The Brāhmaṇas identify Prajāpati with Puruṣa
Both are the creator whose self-sacrifice becomes the cosmos
Vedic Trita (and Avestan Thrita/Thraētaona) continue PIE *Tritós 'the Third'
